title: OKC National Memorial & Museum unveils exhibit featuring iconic Thunder victory parade photo - NewsBreak
text: Thirty years after the 1995 bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building, Oklahoma City is still finding moments of hope. The latest moment was memorialized in an iconic photo of Thunder players in front of the 9:03 Gate during the NBA Finals victory parade. Jimmy Do’s photo is now on display at the Oklahoma City National Memorial & Museum. It's located in the exhibit titled “Hope” and features the significance of the Thunder players in front of the 9:03 Gate. The installation also includes five other significant photos. Earlier this spring, the museum unveiled a revitalized area of Sixth Street to signify a gateway to the memorial and museum . In addition to road improvements, “OKC” and “Be The Light” are illuminated as people drive under the railroad bridge from Interstate 235. About 25 people attended the unveiling ceremony on Wednesday, July 9, including Chair of the Memorial Board Dr. Susan Chambers and Dan Mahoney, Thunder vice president of corporate communications and broadcasting. Both spoke at the event, and Kari Watkins, president and CEO of the Oklahoma City National Memorial & Museum, helped unveil the display. Chambers said museum staff felt honored when the parade route came by the memorial and loved when thousands of people watched the parade from the memorial. “On this street, Robinson, on one end, marks the darkest day in our city’s history, and then just seven blocks away on that very same street, the most triumphant day,” Chambers said. “A day that marks a total renaissance of our city.” More: Carlson: Meet Thunder photographer behind 'one of the most iconic pictures' in OKC history Mahoney talked about seeing the photo for the first time. After a long day of celebrating and still running on a high from the victory, he took a moment to look at Thunder photographers’ work. Among the Thunder’s numerous photographers, videographers and drone pilots, Do’s iconic photo was the first one he saw. “I broke down,” he said. “It was so special ... it kind of brought two phases of my career together, working with Governor Keating and now I was with the Thunder.” Mahoney was former Gov. Frank Keating’s director of communications in 1995. He shared the photo with Watkins, the Thunder executives and his sister in Arizona, he said. The photo received an overwhelmingly positive reaction, and he said requests flooded in with people asking where they could get a copy. Now, the photo is on display at the museum and available for sale in the gift shop and online. “Jimmy Do has the eye of a good photographer, but he’s got the heart of a great photographer,” Mahoney said, adding there was not a more appropriate place for the photo. “We are honored that we have this opportunity to supply this and make sure that people who come to this place see exactly what we all know, which is the resilience of the community and that photo Jimmy took on that slightly warm June afternoon reflects so well. It truly reflects hope over hate, triumph over tragedy,” Mahoney said. More: Thunder fans agreed: OKC parade was 'once in a lifetime' experience they had to attend Do thanked the Thunder organization for putting him in a spot to be able to capture that shot. “It’s a tremendous honor just to be able to capture an image that touches so many people,” he said. Do visited the memorial often when he lived at a nearby apartment building. It has a special place in his heart, he added. “On another level, I think the photo is symbolic of the resiliency of the city, and I love that story being told,” he said. Another image included in the installation is a photo of a Thunder T-shirt with a handwritten note from Sara Sweet and her nephew, Eli Moore, that was placed on her dad's chair in the Field of Empty Chairs at the memorial. The chair honors her father, Stephen Williams, who was killed in the bombing. The new installation encapsulates the city’s progress since the day of the bombing, April 19, 1995. The Thunder’s NBA Finals victory brought a renewed sense of pride and unity to the city, officials with the Oklahoma City National Memorial & Museum said in a news release. Since the team’s arrival in 2008, the Thunder has been steadfast partners and have brought every new player through the museum. Titled "Hope Wins," the image of the Thunder players on the championship bus, paused in front of the 9:03 Gate is a moment filled with grace and reflection, according to the news release. That particular bus, marked with the number 30, traveled in the opposite direction down NW Fifth Street from the path that Timothy McVeigh had taken 30 years ago. “This comparison captures the journey through A Day of Darkness and Years of Light and is proof that Hope Wins,” the memorial said in the news release. This article originally appeared on Oklahoman: OKC National Memorial & Museum unveils exhibit featuring iconic Thunder victory parade photo
